questions.stem: The basic structural and functional unit of the nervous system is the:

options.option_text: Neuron — specialised cell that transmits electrical and chemical signals throughout the body
Nephron — the nephron is the functional unit of the kidney, not the nervous system
Synapse — the synapse is the junction BETWEEN neurons, not the unit itself
Myelin sheath — the myelin sheath is an insulating covering around neuron axons, not the neuron itself

questions.explanation: NEURON: structural + functional unit of the nervous system. PARTS: (1) Cell body (soma) — contains nucleus, metabolic centre. (2) Dendrites — receive signals (multiple, short, branched). (3) Axon — transmits signals away from cell body (single, long). (4) Axon terminals — release neurotransmitters. TYPES: sensory (afferent, receptor→CNS), motor (efferent, CNS→effector), interneurons (connector neurons within CNS). MYELIN SHEATH: lipid insulation around axons (from Schwann cells in PNS, oligodendrocytes in CNS) — speeds up signal transmission. NODES OF RANVIER: gaps in myelin sheath — saltatory conduction occurs here. PYQ: neuron = unit of NS in SSC CGL, IBPS PO, UPSC biology.

questions.stem: A person accidentally touches a hot object and withdraws their hand before consciously feeling pain. This is an example of:

options.option_text: A reflex action — an involuntary rapid response coordinated by the spinal cord, not the brain
A voluntary action — voluntary actions require conscious thought from the cerebral cortex
A conditioned reflex — conditioned reflexes (Pavlov) are learned responses, not innate withdrawal
A hormonal response — hormonal responses are slow (seconds to minutes); reflex is in milliseconds

questions.explanation: REFLEX ARC: receptor → afferent neuron → spinal cord (integration centre) → efferent neuron → effector (muscle). The brain is bypassed for the initial response (but receives the signal afterwards — hence the pain is felt slightly AFTER the hand is pulled away). TYPES: UNCONDITIONED (inborn): knee-jerk, pupillary light reflex, hot-touch withdrawal. CONDITIONED (learned): Pavlov's dog (salivation at bell after training). SPINAL CORD: the integration centre for most spinal reflexes. BRAIN STEM: centre for autonomic reflexes (swallowing, coughing, sneezing). PYQ: reflex action + spinal cord integration in SSC CGL, IBPS PO, UPSC biology.

questions.stem: The cerebellum is responsible primarily for:

options.option_text: Coordination of voluntary muscle movements, balance, and posture
Higher cognitive functions like reasoning, speech, and conscious thought — that is the cerebrum
Regulation of heartbeat, breathing, and blood pressure — that is the medulla oblongata
Processing of visual information from the eyes — that is the occipital lobe of the cerebrum

questions.explanation: BRAIN REGIONS AND FUNCTIONS: CEREBRUM (largest part): intelligence, memory, thought, speech, voluntary movement, sensory processing. CEREBELLUM (hindbrain): COORDINATION, BALANCE, POSTURE — 'fine-tuning' of movements (like walking, playing piano). MEDULLA OBLONGATA: heartbeat, breathing, blood pressure, swallowing, vomiting (vital reflexes). HYPOTHALAMUS: hunger, thirst, body temperature, circadian rhythm, hormone release. THALAMUS: sensory relay station. LIMBIC SYSTEM (hippocampus + amygdala): memory and emotion. PYQ: cerebellum = coordination, balance is a standard 1-marker in SSC CGL, IBPS PO, UPSC.

questions.stem: Acetylcholine (ACh) is a neurotransmitter. When released at the neuromuscular junction, its primary action is to:

options.option_text: Stimulate muscle contraction by binding to receptors on the muscle fibre membrane
Inhibit all nerve signals; acetylcholine is exclusively an inhibitory neurotransmitter
Carry electrical impulses directly across the synaptic cleft without binding to receptors
Transport nutrients from the blood to muscle fibres via the neuromuscular junction

questions.explanation: ACETYLCHOLINE (ACh): the neurotransmitter at neuromuscular junctions (NMJ). Binds to nicotinic receptors on muscle membrane → depolarisation → muscle contraction. CHOLINERGIC SYNAPSES: use ACh. ADRENERGIC SYNAPSES: use adrenaline/noradrenaline. ACh ROLES: (1) NMJ — excitatory (muscle contraction). (2) Parasympathetic NS — excitatory/inhibitory depending on target. (3) CNS — important in memory and attention. MYASTHENIA GRAVIS: autoimmune disease; antibodies block ACh receptors → muscle weakness. ACETYLCHOLINESTERASE: enzyme that breaks down ACh in the synaptic cleft (ending the signal). NERVE GAS (sarin): inhibits acetylcholinesterase → ACh accumulates → continuous muscle spasm. PYQ: ACh + NMJ function in UPSC GS-3, IBPS PO biology.

questions.stem: The autonomic nervous system (ANS) controls involuntary body functions. Its two divisions — sympathetic and parasympathetic — generally have:

options.option_text: Opposing effects on target organs — sympathetic activates (fight-or-flight); parasympathetic calms (rest-and-digest)
The same effects on all organs; they are redundant backup systems for involuntary functions
No effect on the heart; the heart rate is controlled only by hormones like adrenaline (not this)
Effects only on skeletal muscles; smooth muscle and cardiac muscle are under somatic control

questions.explanation: SYMPATHETIC NS (fight-or-flight): increases heart rate, dilates pupils, dilates bronchi, inhibits digestion, increases blood glucose. PARASYMPATHETIC NS (rest-and-digest): decreases heart rate, constricts pupils, promotes digestion, stimulates salivation. NEUROTRANSMITTERS: Sympathetic → noradrenaline (norepinephrine). Parasympathetic → acetylcholine. TARGET ORGANS: both divisions innervate the heart, lungs, GI tract, eyes, glands. DUAL INNERVATION: most organs receive BOTH sympathetic and parasympathetic fibres → antagonistic control allows fine regulation. VAGUS NERVE (CN X): major parasympathetic nerve innervating heart, lungs, GI tract. PYQ: sympathetic vs parasympathetic in UPSC GS-3, IBPS PO biology.

questions.stem: An action potential in a neuron is initiated when:

options.option_text: The membrane potential reaches a threshold value, causing rapid Na+ influx and depolarisation
Potassium ions (K+) rush into the cell, causing the inside to become more positive
The neuron receives any stimulus regardless of strength (no threshold required)
Calcium ions trigger direct muscle contraction without electrical changes in the neuron

questions.explanation: RESTING MEMBRANE POTENTIAL: -70 mV (inside negative). THRESHOLD: ~-55 mV. When a stimulus causes enough depolarisation to reach threshold → voltage-gated Na+ channels open → Na+ rushes IN → inside becomes +30 mV (depolarisation). REPOLARISATION: Na+ channels close; K+ channels open; K+ rushes OUT → inside becomes negative again. HYPERPOLARISATION: K+ channels slow to close → brief undershoot. ALL-OR-NONE LAW: once threshold is reached, action potential is always the same size regardless of stimulus strength. Stronger stimuli produce MORE action potentials per second (frequency coding). REFRACTORY PERIOD: brief period during which another action potential cannot be generated. PYQ: action potential mechanism in UPSC GS-3, NEET-level biology.

questions.stem: Alzheimer's disease is associated with degeneration of neurons that use which neurotransmitter?

options.option_text: Acetylcholine — Alzheimer's involves loss of cholinergic neurons in the basal forebrain (nucleus basalis)
Dopamine — dopamine neuron loss causes Parkinson's disease, not Alzheimer's (not this)
Serotonin — serotonin imbalance is associated with depression and anxiety, not primarily Alzheimer's
GABA — GABA deficiency is linked to epilepsy and anxiety disorders, not Alzheimer's specifically

questions.explanation: ALZHEIMER'S DISEASE: most common form of dementia. NEUROTRANSMITTER: ACETYLCHOLINE — loss of cholinergic neurons in the basal forebrain (nucleus basalis of Meynert) → impaired memory and cognition. HALLMARKS: amyloid plaques (aggregated beta-amyloid protein), neurofibrillary tangles (tau protein). TREATMENT: acetylcholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil, rivastigmine) — slow ACh breakdown to compensate. DOPAMINE diseases: Parkinson's (substantia nigra dopaminergic neurons die → tremor, rigidity). SEROTONIN: mood regulation; SSRIs (fluoxetine) used for depression. GABA: main inhibitory neurotransmitter; benzodiazepines enhance GABA (anti-anxiety). PYQ: Alzheimer's + acetylcholine vs Parkinson's + dopamine in UPSC, IBPS PO science health sections.
